title: Spindel, Weberschiffchen und Nadel
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 188. Text from Wikisource („Spindel, Weberschiffchen und Nadel (1857)“, twice proofread against the original). Fresh translation made directly from the German; 1857 spelling preserved exactly. Contains three blocks of inset verse, two lines each.
about: An orphan girl is left nothing by her dying godmother but a spindle, a shuttle, and a needle, and a small house to use them in. She earns her bread by spinning, weaving, and sewing so faithfully that the tools themselves take a hand in her fortune, spinning thread and weaving cloth that lead a prince straight to her door. It is one of Grimm's gentler tales, where diligence rather than trickery or violence is what is rewarded.

sentences.t: Es war einmal ein Mädchen, dem starb Vater und Mutter, als es noch ein kleines Kind war.
sentences.l: There was once a girl, to whom died father and mother, when it was still a little child.
sentences.i: There was once a girl whose father and mother died while she was still a little child.
sentences.n: dem is a dative relative pronoun — to whom the father and the mother died; German puts the bereaved person in the dative rather than saying her father. das Mädchen is grammatically neuter, so the tale calls the girl es, it, and seine, its, for pages at a time; the English says she.

sentences.t: Am Ende des Dorfes wohnte in einem Häuschen ganz allein seine Pathe, die sich von Spinnen Weben und Nähen ernährte.
sentences.l: At the end of the village lived in a little house quite alone its godmother, who supported herself by spinning, weaving and sewing.
sentences.i: At the end of the village, in a little house, her godmother lived quite alone and made her living by spinning, weaving and sewing.
sentences.n: seine Pathe is its godmother — seine because the girl is neuter. Pathe (modern Pate) served in 1857 for godparent and godchild alike, of either sex; the die that follows and the whole tale show that this one is a woman. “sich von etwas ernähren” is to keep oneself by something; the three infinitives Spinnen, Weben, Nähen stand as nouns.

sentences.t: Die Alte nahm das verlassene Kind zu sich, hielt es zur Arbeit an und erzog es in aller Frömmigkeit.
sentences.l: The old woman took the forsaken child to herself, held it to the work and brought it up in all piety.
sentences.i: The old woman took the forsaken child in, kept it at its work and brought it up in all piety.
sentences.n: “zu sich nehmen” is to take someone into one’s house. anhalten is to keep someone at something, its an waiting at the end of the clause. erziehen is to bring up, rear; the ziehen, to draw, inside it is the same verb used of training a young tree.

sentences.t: Als das Mädchen fünfzehn Jahr alt war, erkrankte sie, rief das Kind an ihr Bett und sagte „liebe Tochter, ich fühle daß mein Ende herannaht,
sentences.l: When the girl was fifteen year old, she fell ill, called the child to her bed and said “dear daughter, I feel that my end draws near,
sentences.i: When the girl was fifteen years old the old woman fell ill, called the child to her bed and said, “Dear daughter, I feel that my end is drawing near;
sentences.n: sie is the old woman, though the girl was named last — German can let the feminine pronoun pick her out, since the girl is neuter. Jahr stays singular after a number, as German does with measures. herannahen is to draw near, with heran at the end. daß is the 1857 spelling of dass.

sentences.t: ich hinterlasse dir das Häuschen, darin bist du vor Wind und Wetter geschützt, dazu Spindel, Weberschiffchen und Nadel, damit kannst du dir dein Brot verdienen.“
sentences.l: I leave behind for you the little house, therein are you protected from wind and weather, in addition spindle, weaver’s-shuttle and needle, with them can you earn yourself your bread.”
sentences.i: I leave you the little house — in it you are safe from wind and weather — and with it the spindle, the shuttle and the needle, and by them you can earn your bread.”
sentences.n: hinterlassen is to leave behind, to bequeath. darin and damit gather a preposition and its pronoun into a single word, in it, with them, and each stands first so that the verb follows straight after. dazu is in addition to that. The three tools are named here once and for all: they are the whole legacy, and from now on they act by themselves.

sentences.t: Sie legte noch die Hände auf seinen Kopf, segnete es und sprach „behalt nur Gott in dem Herzen, so wird dirs wohl gehen.“
sentences.l: She laid still the hands on its head, blessed it and said “only keep God in the heart, so will it go well for you.”
sentences.i: She laid her hands on the girl’s head, blessed her and said, “Only keep God in your heart, and it will go well with you.”
sentences.n: German says die Hände and dem Herzen where English says her hands, your heart — the article is enough once the owner is plain. behalt is the imperative with its -e dropped. nur softens the command to a mere only. “es geht dir wohl” puts the person in the dative, it goes well for you; dirs is dir es.

sentences.t: Darauf schloß sie die Augen, und als sie zur Erde bestattet wurde, gieng das Mädchen bitterlich weinend hinter dem Sarg und erwies ihr die letzte Ehre.
sentences.l: Thereupon she closed the eyes, and when she was buried to the earth, went the girl bitterly weeping behind the coffin and showed her the last honour.
sentences.i: Thereupon she closed her eyes, and when she was laid in the earth the girl walked behind the coffin, weeping bitterly, and paid her the last honour.
sentences.n: “zur Erde bestatten” is the solemn phrase for burial, to lay in the earth. “die letzte Ehre erweisen” is the set phrase for the last respects paid to the dead. gieng is the 1857 spelling of ging.

sentences.t: Das Mädchen lebte nun in dem kleinen Haus ganz allein, war fleißig, spann, webte und nähte, und auf allem, was es that, ruhte der Segen der guten Alten.
sentences.l: The girl lived now in the little house quite alone, was diligent, spun, wove and sewed, and on everything that it did rested the blessing of the good old woman.
sentences.i: The girl lived now in the little house quite alone; she was diligent, she spun and wove and sewed, and on everything she did rested the blessing of the good old woman.
sentences.n: The three trades come back as three verbs — spann, webte, nähte — one for each tool she was left. The phrase “auf allem … ruhte der Segen” is set first for its weight, so the verb ruhte stands ahead of its own subject; the blessing spoken over her head has become something that lies on her work. that is the 1857 spelling of tat.

sentences.t: Es war als ob sich der Flachs in der Kammer von selbst mehrte,
sentences.l: It was as if the flax in the chamber increased of itself,
sentences.i: It was as though the flax in the store-room multiplied of its own accord,
sentences.n: “als ob” takes the subjunctive mehrte — as if it increased, without the tale saying that it did. “von selbst” is of its own accord. der Flachs is the raw flax that has to be spun before there is any thread at all.

sentences.t: und wenn sie ein Stück Tuch oder einen Teppich gewebt, oder ein Hemd genäht hatte, so fand sich gleich ein Käufer, der es reichlich bezahlte, so daß sie keine Noth empfand und andern noch etwas mittheilen konnte.
sentences.l: and when she had woven a piece of cloth or a carpet, or sewn a shirt, so found itself at once a buyer who paid richly for it, so that she felt no want and could impart something still to others.
sentences.i: and whenever she had woven a piece of cloth or a carpet, or sewn a shirt, a buyer was there at once who paid handsomely for it, so that she felt no want and had something over to share with others.
sentences.n: “es fand sich ein Käufer” — a buyer found himself — is German’s way of saying that one simply turned up. The auxiliary hatte is said once and serves both gewebt and genäht. Noth is the 1857 spelling of Not, want. mittheilen, modern mitteilen, is to give someone a share of something.

sentences.t: Um diese Zeit zog der Sohn des Königs im Land umher und wollte sich eine Braut suchen.
sentences.l: About this time drew the son of the king about in the land and wanted to seek himself a bride.
sentences.i: About this time the king’s son was travelling about the country, meaning to look for a bride.
sentences.n: umherziehen is to travel about, its umher standing at the end. “sich eine Braut suchen” has the dative sich — to seek a bride for himself; German likes to mark whom a search is for.

sentences.t: Eine arme sollte er nicht wählen und eine reiche wollte er nicht.
sentences.l: A poor one should he not choose, and a rich one wanted he not.
sentences.i: A poor one he was not to choose, and a rich one he did not want.
sentences.n: arme and reiche are adjectives standing as nouns, a poor one and a rich one, both feminine because a bride is meant. sollte is what others required of him, wollte what he wanted himself, and the sentence sets the two against each other. wählen here is to choose — it is not a form of wollen.

sentences.t: Da sprach er „die soll meine Frau werden, die zugleich die ärmste und die reichste ist.“
sentences.l: Then said he “that one shall become my wife, who at the same time the poorest and the richest is.”
sentences.i: Then he said, “She shall be my wife who is at once the poorest and the richest.”
sentences.n: The first die is a demonstrative, that one, and the second a relative, who; German can set them side by side and English cannot. The riddle he makes for himself here is the whole plot of the tale.

sentences.t: Als er in das Dorf kam, wo das Mädchen lebte, fragte er, wie er überall that, wer in dem Ort die reichste und ärmste wäre.
sentences.l: When he came into the village where the girl lived, asked he, as he everywhere did, who in the place the richest and poorest were.
sentences.i: When he came to the village where the girl lived he asked, as he did everywhere, who in the place was the richest and who the poorest.
sentences.n: wäre is subjunctive because the question is reported rather than put in his own words. der Ort is the place, the locality — a plainer word, used here so that Dorf need not come twice.

sentences.t: Sie nannten ihm die reichste zuerst: die ärmste, sagten sie, wäre das Mädchen, das in dem kleinen Haus ganz am Ende wohnte.
sentences.l: They named to him the richest first: the poorest, said they, were the girl that lived in the little house right at the end.
sentences.i: They named the richest to him first; the poorest, they said, was the girl who lived in the little house right at the end.
sentences.n: wäre again marks reported speech — this is what the villagers said, not what the tale asserts. “ganz am Ende” is right at the end of the village, where we already know the little house stands.

sentences.t: Die Reiche saß vor der Hausthür in vollem Putz, und als der Königssohn sich näherte, stand sie auf, gieng ihm entgegen und neigte sich vor ihm.
sentences.l: The rich one sat before the house-door in full finery, and when the king’s son approached, she stood up, went toward him and bowed herself before him.
sentences.i: The rich one sat before the house door in all her finery, and when the king’s son drew near she stood up, went to meet him and bowed to him.
sentences.n: der Putz is finery, everything put on for show. “jemandem entgegengehen” is to go to meet someone, with entgegen at the end. “sich neigen” is to bend, to curtsey. Hausthür keeps the 1857 th-.

sentences.t: Er sah sie an, sprach kein Wort und ritt weiter.
sentences.l: He looked at her, spoke no word and rode further.
sentences.i: He looked at her, said not a word and rode on.
sentences.n: ansehen, to look at, is separable, and its an waits to the end of the clause: sah sie an. Three quick verbs and no comment — the tale lets the silence do the judging.

sentences.t: Als er zu dem Haus der Armen kam, stand das Mädchen nicht an der Thüre, sondern saß in seinem Stübchen.
sentences.l: When he came to the house of the poor one, the girl stood not at the door, but sat in its little room.
sentences.i: When he came to the poor one’s house the girl was not standing at the door but sitting in her little room.
sentences.n: der Armen is the genitive of die Arme, the poor one — the same adjective-as-noun as before. sondern is the but that follows a negative and puts something in its place. Stübchen is the diminutive of Stube; seinem is its, the girl being neuter.

sentences.t: Er hielt das Pferd an und sah durch das Fenster, durch das die helle Sonne schien, das Mädchen an dem Spinnrad sitzen und emsig spinnen.
sentences.l: He held the horse up and saw through the window, through which the bright sun shone, the girl at the spinning-wheel sit and busily spin.
sentences.i: He reined in his horse and saw through the window, through which the bright sun was shining, the girl sitting at her spinning wheel and spinning busily.
sentences.n: anhalten is to bring to a stop, an at the end. After sehen German uses the bare infinitives sitzen and spinnen where English needs sitting and spinning. emsig is busily, industriously — an old word and always praise.

sentences.t: Es blickte auf, und als es bemerkte daß der Königssohn hereinschaute, ward es über und über roth, schlug die Augen nieder und spann weiter;
sentences.l: It looked up, and when it noticed that the king’s son looked in, became it over and over red, struck the eyes down and spun further;
sentences.i: She looked up, and when she saw that the king’s son was looking in she turned red all over, cast her eyes down and went on spinning;
sentences.n: ward is the old past of werden, became. “über und über” is all over, from top to toe. “die Augen niederschlagen” is the set phrase for casting the eyes down. hereinschauen is to look in from outside, toward the person spoken of.

sentences.t: ob der Faden diesmal ganz gleich ward, weiß ich nicht, aber es spann so lange bis der Königssohn wieder weggeritten war.
sentences.l: whether the thread this time quite even became, know I not, but it spun so long until the king’s son had ridden away again.
sentences.i: whether the thread came out quite even this time I do not know, but she spun on until the king’s son had ridden away again.
sentences.n: weiß here is the verb wissen, I know — not the adjective weiß, white, which turns up in this same tale for the feathers in his hat; the spelling is the same and only the sentence tells them apart. The teller steps forward for one clause to say what the tale does not know. gleich is even, uniform, said of a well-spun thread.

sentences.t: Dann trat es ans Fenster, öffnete es und sagte „es ist so heiß in der Stube,“ aber es blickte ihm nach so lange es noch die weißen Federn an seinem Hut erkennen konnte.
sentences.l: Then stepped it to the window, opened it and said “it is so hot in the room,” but it looked after him so long as it could still make out the white feathers on his hat.
sentences.i: Then she stepped to the window, opened it and said, “It is so hot in the room” — but she looked after him as long as she could still make out the white feathers on his hat.
sentences.n: Three es in one sentence, each a different thing: the girl, the window she opens, and the impersonal es of “es ist heiß.” “jemandem nachblicken” is to gaze after someone, nach at the end. She says one thing and does another, and the tale makes no comment.

sentences.t: Das Mädchen setzte sich wieder in seine Stube zur Arbeit und spann weiter.
sentences.l: The girl set itself again in its room to the work and spun further.
sentences.i: The girl sat down again in her room to her work and went on spinning.
sentences.n: “sich setzen” is to sit oneself down; the reflexive sich is what makes it an act rather than a state. “zur Arbeit” — to the work — gives the purpose of sitting down.

sentences.t: Da kam ihm ein Spruch in den Sinn, den die Alte manchmal gesagt hatte, wenn es bei der Arbeit saß, und es sang so vor sich hin
sentences.l: Then came to it a saying into the mind, which the old woman sometimes had said when it sat at the work, and it sang so before itself along
sentences.i: Then a rhyme came into her mind that the old woman used to say when she sat at her work, and she sang it quietly to herself
sentences.n: “jemandem kommt etwas in den Sinn” puts the person in the dative: something comes into the mind to her. ein Spruch is a saying or set rhyme, the kind spoken over work. “vor sich hin singen” is to sing to oneself, half aloud, with hin at the end. The sentence ends without a full stop because the couplet follows straight on.

sentences.t:
„Spindel, Spindel, geh du aus,
bring den Freier in mein Haus.“
sentences.l:
“Spindle, spindle, go you out,
bring the suitor into my house.”
sentences.i:
“Spindle, spindle, out you go,
bring the suitor into my house.”
sentences.n: The German couplet rhymes aus with Haus, and each of the three songs in this tale rhymes on the last word of its second line; the English here is left unrhymed so that the words can stand as they are. “geh du aus” sets du after the imperative for emphasis — out you go. der Freier is the suitor, the man who comes courting.

sentences.t: Was geschah?
sentences.l: What happened?
sentences.n: The teller turns to the reader for one breath before the wonder, and no one answers. geschehen is to happen, to come to pass.

sentences.t: Die Spindel sprang ihm augenblicklich aus der Hand und zur Thüre hinaus;
sentences.l: The spindle sprang to it instantly out of the hand and to the door out;
sentences.i: The spindle leapt from her hand that instant and out at the door;
sentences.n: ihm is the dative of the person it happens to — sprang out of the hand, to her; German prefers this to saying her hand. “zur Thüre hinaus” is out through the door, hinaus marking the motion away.

sentences.t: und als es vor Verwunderung aufstand und ihr nachblickte, so sah es daß sie lustig in das Feld hinein tanzte und einen glänzenden goldenen Faden hinter sich herzog.
sentences.l: and when it stood up from astonishment and looked after it, so saw it that it merrily into the field in danced and drew a gleaming golden thread behind itself along.
sentences.i: and when she stood up in astonishment and looked after it, she saw it dancing merrily out into the field and drawing a gleaming golden thread along behind it.
sentences.n: vor here is out of, from — vor Verwunderung, out of astonishment. The spindle is sie because die Spindel is feminine. herziehen is to draw something along behind one, its her at the end; the same spelling herzog is elsewhere in the KHM the noun Herzog, a duke, and it is not that here.

sentences.t: Nicht lange, so war sie ihm aus den Augen entschwunden.
sentences.l: Not long, and it had vanished to her out of the eyes.
sentences.i: Before long it had vanished from her sight.
sentences.n: “nicht lange, so …” is a set narrative turn — it was not long before. entschwinden is to vanish away, a lifted word. ihm is once more the dative of the person concerned: out of the eyes, to her.

sentences.t: Das Mädchen, da es keine Spindel mehr hatte, nahm das Weberschiffchen in die Hand, setzte sich an den Webstuhl und fieng an zu weben.
sentences.l: The girl, since it had no spindle any more, took the weaver’s-shuttle into the hand, set itself at the loom and began to weave.
sentences.i: The girl, since she had no spindle any longer, took the shuttle in her hand, sat down at the loom and began to weave.
sentences.n: da here is since, because — not there. das Weberschiffchen is the weaver’s little ship: the boat-shaped shuttle that carries the cross-thread through the loom. The second tool takes over the moment the first is gone.

sentences.t: Die Spindel aber tanzte immer weiter, und eben als der Faden zu Ende war, hatte sie den Königssohn erreicht.
sentences.l: The spindle however danced ever further, and just as the thread was at an end, had it reached the king’s son.
sentences.i: The spindle, meanwhile, went on dancing, and just as the thread came to an end it had reached the king’s son.
sentences.n: aber in second place is less but than however, meanwhile; it turns the story to the other party. “immer weiter” is on and on. eben is just, exactly at that moment.

sentences.t: „Was sehe ich?“ rief er, „die Spindel will mir wohl den Weg zeigen?“
sentences.l: “What do I see?” cried he, “the spindle wants surely to show me the way?”
sentences.i: “What do I see?” he cried. “The spindle means to show me the way, does it not?”
sentences.n: wohl marks a guess rather than a fact — I suppose, surely. wollen said of a thing is not wanting but intending, being about to. The words keep the order of a plain statement and only the question mark makes them a question.

sentences.t: drehte sein Pferd um und ritt an dem goldenen Faden zurück.
sentences.l: turned his horse around and rode along the golden thread back.
sentences.i: He turned his horse about and rode back along the golden thread.
sentences.n: The subject he is not said again after the speech — German lets the sentence run straight on from rief er. umdrehen and zurückreiten are both separable, and um and zurück each wait at the end of their clause.

sentences.t: Das Mädchen aber saß an seiner Arbeit und sang
sentences.l: The girl however sat at its work and sang
sentences.i: The girl, meanwhile, sat at her work and sang
sentences.n: The tale cuts back to the cottage with the same aber that took it away. Again there is no full stop: the song follows.

sentences.t:
„Schiffchen, Schiffchen, webe fein,
führ den Freier mir herein.“
sentences.l:
“Little-shuttle, little-shuttle, weave fine,
lead the suitor in here to me.”
sentences.i:
“Shuttle, shuttle, weave finely,
bring the suitor in to me.”
sentences.n: führ is the imperative of führen, to lead or bring — not a form of fahren. herein is in, toward the speaker, so the suitor is to be brought in here to her. The German rhymes fein with herein; the English does not rhyme.

sentences.t: Alsbald sprang ihr das Schiffchen aus der Hand und sprang zur Thüre hinaus.
sentences.l: At once sprang to her the shuttle out of the hand and sprang to the door out.
sentences.i: At once the shuttle leapt from her hand and out at the door.
sentences.n: Almost word for word the spindle’s sentence: the tale is built of three matching turns. alsbald is at once, an old and formal word. Here the girl is ihr, the feminine dative, though elsewhere she is the neuter ihm — the 1857 text does both, sometimes within a page.

sentences.t: Vor der Thürschwelle aber fieng es an einen Teppich zu weben, schöner als man je einen gesehen hat.
sentences.l: Before the threshold however began it a carpet to weave, more beautiful than one has ever seen one.
sentences.i: But in front of the threshold it began to weave a carpet more beautiful than any that has ever been seen.
sentences.n: es is the shuttle, das Schiffchen being neuter. “als man je einen gesehen hat” keeps the present perfect and reaches down to the reader’s own day: than one has ever seen. man is the impersonal one, anybody.

sentences.t: Auf beiden Seiten blühten Rosen und Lilien und in der Mitte auf goldenem Grund stiegen grüne Ranken herauf,
sentences.l: On both sides bloomed roses and lilies, and in the middle on golden ground climbed green tendrils up,
sentences.i: On both sides roses and lilies bloomed, and in the middle, on a golden ground, green tendrils climbed up,
sentences.n: der Grund is the ground of a picture or a weaving, the background the figures stand on. Each phrase of place comes first and pushes its verb ahead of its subject — bloomed roses, climbed tendrils. heraufsteigen is to climb up toward the viewer, herauf at the end.

sentences.t: darin sprangen Hasen und Kaninchen: Hirsche und Rehe streckten die Köpfe dazwischen: oben in den Zweigen saßen bunte Vögel; es fehlte nichts als daß sie gesungen hätten.
sentences.l: therein sprang hares and rabbits: stags and roe-deer stretched the heads in between: above in the branches sat brightly-coloured birds; there lacked nothing except that they had sung.
sentences.i: in among them sprang hares and rabbits; stags and roe deer put their heads out between; above, in the branches, sat brightly coloured birds — nothing was wanting but that they should sing.
sentences.n: The colons are the 1857 printing’s way of stringing pictures together where we would use semicolons. “es fehlte nichts als daß …” is nothing was lacking except that; hätten is subjunctive, so the singing is precisely what does not happen.

sentences.t: Das Schiffchen sprang hin und her, und es war als wüchse alles von selber.
sentences.l: The shuttle sprang hither and thither, and it was as if everything grew of itself.
sentences.i: The shuttle leapt to and fro, and it was as though everything grew of its own accord.
sentences.n: “hin und her” is to and fro — hin away from the speaker, her toward. wüchse is the past subjunctive of wachsen after als: as if it grew, with no claim that it did.

sentences.t: Weil das Schiffchen fortgelaufen war, hatte sich das Mädchen zum Nähen hingesetzt: es hielt die Nadel in der Hand und sang
sentences.l: Because the shuttle had run off, had the girl set itself down to the sewing: it held the needle in the hand and sang
sentences.i: Since the shuttle had run off, the girl had sat down to her sewing; she held the needle in her hand and sang
sentences.n: fortlaufen is to run away, said of the shuttle as of a living thing — all three tools are creatures here, with wills of their own. “sich hinsetzen” is to sit oneself down, hin at the end. Nähen is the infinitive used as a noun, the sewing.

sentences.t:
„Nadel, Nadel, spitz und fein,
Mach das Haus dem Freier rein.“
sentences.l:
“Needle, needle, sharp and fine,
make the house for the suitor clean.”
sentences.i:
“Needle, needle, sharp and fine,
make the house clean for the suitor.”
sentences.n: “rein machen” is to make clean, to put in order, and German splits the two words with rein at the end. dem Freier is a dative of interest — clean for the suitor, on his account. The German rhymes fein with rein, keeping the shape of the first two songs; the capital M of Mach is the 1857 printing’s own.

sentences.t: Da sprang ihr die Nadel aus den Fingern und flog in der Stube hin und her, so schnell wie der Blitz.
sentences.l: Then sprang to her the needle out of the fingers and flew in the room to and fro, as fast as the lightning.
sentences.i: Then the needle leapt from her fingers and flew about the room, as quick as lightning.
sentences.n: The third tool goes the way of the first two, and the sentence is built to match theirs. German says der Blitz with its article where English has lightning bare.

sentences.t: Es war nicht anders als wenn unsichtbare Geister arbeiteten,
sentences.l: It was not otherwise than as if invisible spirits worked,
sentences.i: It was just as though invisible spirits were at work,
sentences.n: “nicht anders als wenn” — not otherwise than if — is a weightier way of saying just as if. arbeiteten is again the subjunctive that keeps a comparison from becoming a claim.

sentences.t: alsbald überzogen sich Tisch und Bänke mit grünem Tuch, die Stühle mit Sammet, und an den Fenstern hiengen seidene Vorhänge herab.
sentences.l: at once covered themselves table and benches with green cloth, the chairs with velvet, and at the windows hung silken curtains down.
sentences.i: at once table and benches covered themselves with green cloth, the chairs with velvet, and silken curtains hung down at the windows.
sentences.n: “sich überziehen mit” is to become covered with something, the furniture doing it to itself. The verb for the chairs is left out and understood from the clause before. Sammet is the older form of Samt, velvet; hiengen is the 1857 spelling of hingen.

sentences.t: Kaum hatte die Nadel den letzten Stich gethan, so sah das Mädchen schon durch das Fenster die weißen Federn von dem Hut des Königssohns, den die Spindel an dem goldenen Faden herbei geholt hatte.
sentences.l: Hardly had the needle done the last stitch, so saw the girl already through the window the white feathers from the hat of the king’s son, whom the spindle on the golden thread had fetched here.
sentences.i: Hardly had the needle taken the last stitch when the girl saw through the window the white feathers on the king’s son’s hat — the son whom the spindle had fetched along the golden thread.
sentences.n: “kaum … so …” is hardly … when. der Stich is a stitch in sewing, the same word that elsewhere means a stab. gethan is the 1857 spelling of getan. den is masculine accusative and so points back to the king’s son, not to the hat.

sentences.t: Er stieg ab, schritt über den Teppich in das Haus herein, und als er in die Stube trat, stand das Mädchen da in seinem ärmlichen Kleid, aber es glühte darin wie eine Rose im Busch.
sentences.l: He climbed down, strode over the carpet into the house in, and when he stepped into the room, stood the girl there in its poor dress, but it glowed therein like a rose in the bush.
sentences.i: He dismounted, strode over the carpet and into the house, and when he stepped into the room the girl stood there in her poor dress, but she glowed in it like a rose in the bush.
sentences.n: schritt is the past of schreiten, to stride — not the noun der Schritt, a step. absteigen is to get down from a horse. ärmlich is poor in the sense of shabby and meagre, and it is the word the tale has kept for her all along.

sentences.t: „Du bist die Ärmste und auch die Reichste,“ sprach er zu ihr, „komm mit mir, du sollst meine Braut sein.“
sentences.l: “You are the poorest and also the richest,” said he to her, “come with me, you shall be my bride.”
sentences.i: “You are the poorest and also the richest,” he said to her. “Come with me; you shall be my bride.”
sentences.n: He speaks to her as du, the close and plain form — it is you, never any older English pronoun. The riddle he set himself at the start is answered here in his own words, with the capitals of Ärmste and Reichste as the 1857 text prints them.

sentences.t: Sie schwieg, aber sie reichte ihm die Hand.
sentences.l: She kept silent, but she reached him the hand.
sentences.i: She said nothing, but she gave him her hand.
sentences.n: schweigen is not merely to be quiet but to hold one’s peace, a chosen silence. “jemandem die Hand reichen” is to hold out one’s hand to someone; here it is her whole answer, and the tale gives her no words at all.

sentences.t: Da gab er ihr einen Kuß, führte sie hinaus, hob sie auf sein Pferd und brachte sie in das königliche Schloß, wo die Hochzeit mit großer Freude gefeiert ward.
sentences.l: Then gave he her a kiss, led her out, lifted her onto his horse and brought her into the royal castle, where the wedding with great joy was celebrated.
sentences.i: Then he gave her a kiss, led her out, lifted her onto his horse and brought her to the royal castle, where the wedding was celebrated with great joy.
sentences.n: hob is from heben, to lift, and the auf beside it is the preposition onto, not a particle of the verb. ward with a past participle is the old passive — was celebrated.

sentences.t: Spindel, Weberschiffchen und Nadel wurden in der Schatzkammer verwahrt und in großen Ehren gehalten.
sentences.l: Spindle, weaver’s-shuttle and needle were kept in the treasure-chamber and held in great honours.
sentences.i: Spindle, shuttle and needle were kept in the treasure chamber and held in great honour.
sentences.n: The three tools are named in the order in which they were left to her, and they close the tale as they opened it. “in Ehren halten” is to hold in honour, where German has the plural Ehren and English the singular. verwahren is to put away in safety.

glossary.aufstand: aufstehen — stood up (3rd sg. preterite; separable auf-)
glossary.drehte: drehen — turned (3rd sg. preterite; drehte … um, umdrehen, to turn round)
glossary.führ: führen — bring, lead (imperative sg.; führ … herein: bring in here)
glossary.gesungen: singen — sung (past part.; gesungen hätten, had sung — past subjunctive)
glossary.grund: der Grund — ground, base; the background of a picture or a weaving
glossary.hob: heben — lifted, raised (3rd sg. preterite; with the particle auf it is aufheben, to pick up)
glossary.mach: machen — make, do (imperative sg.; mach … rein, rein machen, to make clean)
glossary.pathe: die Pathe — godmother (1857 spelling; Pathe, modern Pate, serves for godparent and godchild of either sex)
glossary.reiche: reich — the rich one (adjective used as a noun, feminine; the same spelling is also reichen, to hand, to reach)
glossary.schiffchen: das Schiffchen — the weaver’s shuttle (literally a little ship, from its shape)
glossary.schritt: schreiten — strode, stepped (3rd sg. preterite; the same spelling is also der Schritt, a step)
glossary.stich: der Stich — stitch (in sewing; the same word also means a prick or stab)
glossary.streckten: strecken — stretched out, put out (3rd pl. preterite)
glossary.ward: werden — became, was (3rd sg. past, archaic for wurde; also the passive auxiliary, was …ed)
glossary.weiß: wissen — know (1st sg. present, ich weiß; the same spelling is also the adjective weiß, white)
glossary.zog: umherziehen — travelled about (3rd sg. preterite; zog … umher; ziehen by itself is to draw, to pull)
glossary.überzogen: überziehen — covered over (3rd pl. preterite here; sich überziehen mit: to become covered with)
